stem:
A patient has sustained return of spontaneous circulation after cardiac arrest and is ventilated in the emergency department. Pulse oximetry now has a reliable waveform and reads 100% while the inspired oxygen fraction is 1.0. The emergency registrar is adjusting oxygen as part of post-arrest care.

Which strategy is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Titrate inspired oxygen to an initial saturation of 94–98%
options.explanation: After reliable oxygenation measurements are available, ANZCOR recommends an initial target saturation of 94–98%, avoiding both hypoxaemia and unnecessary hyperoxaemia.

options.label: B
options.text: Leave the inspired oxygen fraction at 1.0 until a blood gas returns
options.explanation: A reliable oximetry waveform is enough to start titrating. Holding FiO2 at 1.0 until a gas returns prolongs avoidable hyperoxaemia; the arterial gas then refines the target.

options.label: C
options.text: Continue maximal FiO2 for the first 24 hours
options.explanation: Maximal oxygen is appropriate during CPR and until reliable measurement is available. Continuing it for a fixed period after ROSC exposes the patient to avoidable hyperoxaemia.

options.label: D
options.text: Aim lower, at 88–92%, to minimise hyperoxic injury
options.explanation: A lower range may apply to selected patients with a separate risk of hypercapnic failure, but it is not the routine initial post-arrest target described by ANZCOR.

options.label: E
options.text: Keep SpO2 at 98–100% to maximise tissue delivery
options.explanation: A saturation of 100% cannot distinguish normoxia from marked hyperoxaemia, so a 98–100% target risks the hyperoxaemia post-arrest care aims to avoid. ANZCOR sets an initial target of 94–98%.

context: After ROSC, use reliable monitoring to titrate oxygen towards 94–98% rather than continuing maximal oxygen by default.
